title: Supply
summary: The law of supply says quantity supplied rises with price. Non-price determinants shift supply. HL adds diminishing marginal returns and linear supply functions.

keyterms.definition: The quantity of a good firms are willing and able to produce and sell at each possible price over a time period, ceteris paribus.
As the price of a good rises, quantity supplied rises, ceteris paribus: a positive relationship.
The sum of all individual firms’ supply at each price.
Payments for inputs such as wages, raw materials and energy; higher costs shift supply left.
A tax on spending on goods and services, paid to government by the seller; it shifts supply left (up).
A payment by government to producers per unit or in total; it lowers costs and shifts supply right.
When producing one good automatically produces another, e.g. beef and leather.
When producers can switch resources between goods, so more of one means less of another, e.g. wheat and corn.
Firms’ beliefs about future prices; expecting higher prices may cause them to hold back supply now.
The period in which at least one factor of production is fixed.
In the short run, as more of a variable factor is added to a fixed factor, the extra output from each unit eventually falls.
The extra cost of producing one more unit of output.
An equation Qs = c + dP, where d > 0 shows how quantity supplied responds to price.

lessons.title: The law of supply and its determinants

questions.prompt: Why does the supply curve usually slope upward?
options: Consumers buy more at higher prices
Higher prices make production more profitable and cover rising costs
questions.explanation: Higher prices give an incentive to produce more and allow firms to cover the higher cost of extra output.

questions.statement: A rise in wages paid to workers in the clothing industry shifts the supply curve of clothing to the right.
questions.explanation: Higher costs reduce supply at every price: the curve shifts left.

questions.prompt: Which would shift the supply of rice to the right?
options: A rise in the price of rice
A new indirect tax on rice
questions.explanation: Better technology lowers costs. A higher rice price is a movement; a tax and a flood shift supply left.

questions.text: A government payment to producers that lowers their costs is a ___.
questions.explanation: Subsidies shift supply right (down) by the amount of the subsidy per unit.

questions.prompt: Match each event to its effect on the supply of cars.
questions.explanation: Own price moves along the curve; costs, technology, taxes and subsidies shift it.

questions.statement: Beef and leather are in joint supply: more beef production automatically raises leather supply.
questions.explanation: They come from the same animal, so supply of one rises with the other.

questions.prompt: A farmer can grow either wheat or barley. The price of barley rises. What happens to the supply of wheat?
options: It shifts left as land is switched to barley
Quantity supplied of wheat rises along the curve
questions.explanation: Wheat and barley are in competitive supply; resources move to the more profitable crop.

questions.text: Adding together the supply of every firm at each price gives ___ supply.
questions.explanation: Market supply is the horizontal sum of individual firms’ supply curves.

questions.prompt: Oil producers expect prices to rise sharply next month. What is the likely effect on supply today?
options: Supply today decreases as they hold back output
questions.explanation: Firms may store output to sell later at a higher price, shifting current supply left.

questions.prompt: Order the effects of a per-unit indirect tax on sugar.
items: Government levies a tax per kilo sold
Equilibrium price rises and quantity falls
questions.explanation: A specific tax raises costs per unit, shifting supply up by the tax amount and creating a new equilibrium.

lessons.title: HL: diminishing returns and supply functions

questions.prompt: The law of diminishing marginal returns applies…
options: in the short run, when at least one factor is fixed
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns occur because a variable factor is added to a fixed factor.

questions.statement: Because of diminishing marginal returns, marginal cost eventually rises as output increases.
questions.explanation: If each extra worker adds less output, each extra unit of output costs more to produce.

questions.text: The extra cost of producing one more unit is ___ cost.
questions.explanation: Rising marginal cost explains why firms need a higher price to supply more in the short run.

questions.prompt: A bakery with one oven hires workers: total output is 20, 45, 65, 80 loaves with 1, 2, 3, 4 workers. When do diminishing marginal returns begin?
questions.explanation: Marginal products are 20, 25, 20, 15. MP starts falling with the 3rd worker.

questions.prompt: Given Qs = −20 + 5P, what is quantity supplied at P = 12?
For Qs = −20 + 5P, below what price will nothing be supplied?
questions.explanation: Set 0 = −20 + 5P, so P = 4. This is the price intercept of supply.

questions.statement: A subsidy to producers would raise the "c" term in Qs = c + dP.
questions.explanation: More is supplied at every price, so the constant rises and the curve shifts right.

questions.text: Qs = 10 + 4P. If price rises by $3, quantity supplied rises by ___ units.
questions.explanation: Each $1 adds 4 units, so $3 adds 12.

questions.prompt: Match each concept to its description.

pairs.right: At least one factor is fixed
Falling extra output from a variable factor

questions.explanation: Diminishing returns raise marginal cost, which underlies the upward-sloping short-run supply curve.

questions.prompt: Order the chain explaining why short-run supply slopes upward.
items: Extra workers add less and less output
Firms need higher prices to supply more
questions.explanation: Diminishing marginal returns raise marginal cost, so a higher price is needed to make extra output worthwhile.
